title: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But there are no obvious mechanical forces by which we can so explain this peculiar polarity. This at least is evident, that it arises in the central mass of protoplasm, which is the essential living portion of the organism

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IX, “On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons”; topic “Polarity and Lehmann's fluid crystals”. Scope: Radiolaria with fixed numbers and positions of radial spines (Acantharia, Phaeodaria)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch09-19: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.26

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A modernized central-versus-peripheral origin can be tested, but Thompson's positive force concept is underspecified. Existing mature morphology cannot establish temporal or causal origin, making new developmental data necessary.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In developing Radiolaria, temporally map polarity markers, central cytoplasmic organization, peripheral vesicles and nascent spines, then perturb candidate central and peripheral mechanisms. The claim predicts central polarity before spine placement and persistence when peripheral mechanics are altered.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Absence of an obvious peripheral mechanism is not evidence for a central force.

The proposed 'directive forces' have no unique modern observable.

Developmental perturbation data for these organisms are lacking.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The passage states that no obvious mechanical account is available and points to fluid crystals as a direction in which to look, which does not fix variables or a decision rule. Adult skeletons show the polarity without showing where it was generated or which force class produced it. Existing images are compatible with the suggestion and with its rivals, so the claim as stated is not an empirical contrast.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: No outcome cleanly separates an unexplained central polarity, said to be perhaps like fluid-crystal directive forces, from other ways of placing a fixed set of spines. Locating the first sign of polarity in the central cytoplasm would address only that geographical clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Central origin, cortical origin and several molecular polarities can leave the same adult spine map.

Absence of an obvious mechanical force is not a measurement with a refuting result.
